known_facts_book1: Exists only inside the poem Tweedledee recites; he never meets Alice and never appears in the story itself.
Walks close at hand with the Carpenter and weeps to see such quantities of sand.
Beseeches the Oysters to come and walk with them along the briny beach, saying they cannot do with more than four.
Proposes to talk of shoes and ships and sealing-wax, of cabbages and kings, and why the sea is boiling hot.
Says a loaf of bread is what they chiefly need, with pepper and vinegar besides.
Weeps and deeply sympathizes while sorting out the oysters of the largest size behind his pocket handkerchief.
Alice likes him best for being a little sorry for the oysters, until Tweedledee points out he ate more than the Carpenter under cover of the handkerchief.

known_relations_book1.Carpenter: His companion on the beach; they eat every one of the oysters between them.
known_relations_book1.Tweedledee: The brother who recites the poem he lives in.
known_relations_book1.Oysters: The four and four and more that follow him from the oyster-bed and are eaten.

known_facts_book1: Exists only inside the poem Tweedledee recites; he never meets Alice and never appears in the story itself.
Doubts that seven maids with seven mops could sweep the sand clear in half a year, and sheds a bitter tear.
Says 'No hurry!' to the oysters, and is thanked much for it.
Says nothing but 'Cut us another slice' and 'The butter's spread too thick!'
Asks the oysters whether they shall be trotting home again, when there is no one left to answer.
Alice likes him best after the Walrus is exposed, until Tweedledum says he ate as many as he could get.

known_relations_book1.Walrus: His companion; the two of them eat every oyster.
known_relations_book1.Tweedledee: The brother whose recitation he exists in.
known_relations_book1.Oysters: The victims of the pleasant walk and pleasant talk.

known_facts_book1: Exist only inside the poem Tweedledee recites.
The eldest Oyster looks at the Walrus, winks his eye and shakes his heavy head, meaning that he did not choose to leave the oyster-bed.
Four young oysters hurry up with their coats brushed and their shoes clean and neat, though they hadn't any feet, and four more follow, and then more and more.
Beg for a bit of time before the chat because some are out of breath and all of them are fat.
Cry 'But not on us!' and turn a little blue when the Walrus calls for bread, pepper and vinegar.
Are all eaten: 'answer came there none—And that was scarcely odd, because They'd eaten every one.'

known_relations_book1.Walrus: Lured from the oyster-bed by his beseeching and eaten by him.
known_relations_book1.Carpenter: The other eater, who complains only about the butter.
